sentences.text: Things go missing at Skálanes and everybody knows which things.
Not tools.
Not keys, not phones, not the small metal objects that vanish in every house on earth.
What goes missing at Skálanes, and has gone missing for as long as anybody can produce a complaint about it, is anything made of wool.
Gloves, principally.
Ari's mother reckons the household has lost somewhere between four and nine gloves a year since he was born, which over twelve years is a number she does not like saying out loud.
There is a box in the porch at Skálanes with about thirty single gloves in it.
Every farm on that road has one.

It is understood in that part of Iceland that you do not throw away a widowed glove, because the other one might come back, and about one in six of them does — turning up in a ditch in the spring, or under a fence, or once, memorably, folded on a gatepost.
Also: a hat off a fence post.
Three pairs of socks off the line, always the socks and never the shirts.
The lining out of a boot.
Half a sheepskin that was under the back door for people to wipe their feet on and that was there on a Tuesday and gone on a Wednesday, and which weighed about four kilos.
The village had a theory and the theory was the wind, which is not a stupid theory in a place where the wind takes roofs.
It accounted for most of it.
Anything on a line, anything on a wall, anything left on the seat of the quad — the wind at Skálanes will take all of that and has taken a trampoline.
Nobody had ever had to look any further, because the wind is a complete explanation that requires no thought and is right about eight times out of ten.
Ari stopped believing it at eleven for a reason that had nothing to do with anything clever.
He watched a glove go.

It was on the wall by the byre, in April, in a dead calm — the first properly still day of that year, so still that the smoke from the Hansdóttir chimney was going straight up — and he was thirty metres away doing something with a bucket, and he looked up because of the movement, and there was a glove going along the top of the wall about a foot above the stone.
Under it, going at a fast trot with her head up and the glove in her teeth, was a fox.
She was in the blue phase — grey-brown in summer, small, low, with the short round ears they have — and she was not skulking.
She went along the base of that wall in full daylight thirty metres from a boy with a bucket at a pace that said she had somewhere to be and had done this route a great many times.
Ari stood there with the bucket until she was out of sight, which took about forty seconds, and then went in and said nothing to anybody for the rest of the day.
